chapter_summary:
Particle systems are incredibly versatile in computer graphics, used for everything from smoke, fire, and water splashes to sand, dust, and abstract effects. In Houdini, particle simulations are handled within the POPs (Particle Operators) context, which resides inside a `POP Network` node, itself typically placed within a `DOP Network`. The core idea behind POPs is to simulate a multitude of individual points, each with its own properties (position, velocity, color, age, etc.), that interact with forces, colliders, and each other. Unlike rigid bodies, particles are often treated as massless or very low-mass entities, and their primary characteristic is their sheer number.

The starting point for any particle system is a `POP Source` node. This node defines how and where particles are born. You can emit particles from geometry (e.g., from the surface or volume of a sphere), from points, or even from specific locations. Key parameters on the `POP Source` include `Emission Type` (e.g., `Scatter on Surface`, `Points`), `Birth Rate` (how many particles per second), `Life Expectancy` (how long particles live), and `Velocity` (initial speed and direction). Once particles are born, their movement and behavior are governed by a `POP Solver` and various `POP Force` nodes. The `POP Solver` is analogous to the `RBD Solver`, advancing the particle simulation frame by frame. Common `POP Force` nodes include `POP Wind` for directional forces, `POP Drag` to simulate air resistance, and `POP Attract` to pull particles towards a point or object.

Collisions are just as important for particles as they are for rigid bodies. Particles need to interact with the environment, bouncing off surfaces or accumulating in containers. You achieve this by adding `Static Object` nodes (for immovable colliders) or `RBD Packed Object` nodes (for dynamic colliders) to your DOP network, ensuring they are merged into the `POP Solver`. Additionally, specific POP nodes like `POP Collision Detect` can be used within the `POP Network` to fine-tune collision responses, such as `Bounce` and `Friction`. A particularly interesting application of POPs is `POP Grains`. This node allows particles to behave like a granular material, such as sand or sugar, where individual particles try to maintain a certain distance from their neighbors, creating a fluid-like or pile-up effect. When you enable `POP Grains`, particles gain a sense of volume and repulsion, making them suitable for simulating pouring sand, dissolving sugar cubes, or even viscous liquids.

Understanding particle attributes is fundamental for advanced control. Every particle carries a set of attributes, much like geometry points in SOPs. The most common are `P` (position), `v` (velocity), `id` (a unique identifier for each particle), and `age` (how long the particle has been alive). You can visualize these attributes in the viewport and even modify them using `POP Wrangle` or `POP VOP` nodes, similar to `Point Wrangle` in SOPs. For instance, you might use `age` to control a particle's color or size over its lifetime, or `v` to drive a motion blur effect. Common mistakes in POPs often involve forgetting to connect the `POP Source` to the `POP Solver`, or not merging collision objects into the DOP network correctly, leading to particles passing through geometry. Another common issue is having too low a `Birth Rate` for the desired effect, or conversely, too high a rate, leading to slow simulations. Always start with a lower birth rate and gradually increase it.

screens.title: Introduction to Particle Systems — POP Grains
screens.subtitle: How Houdini simulates thousands of interacting points to create sand, dust, and fluid-like behavior.

narration.text: In this chapter you'll explore how Houdini models particle systems using POPs and how POP Grains lets particles behave like sand or granular fluids. We'll start with the core idea: particles are many simple points, each carrying attributes such as position, velocity, identity, and life span. You'll learn to emit particles from geometry with a POP Source, advance their motion with a POP Solver and forces, and make them pile and flow using POP Grains. I'll walk you through a hands-on lab that uses a sphere emitter and a tube container so you see particles pour, collide and accumulate. Along the way we'll cover collisions, typical force nodes like wind and drag, and how to inspect and modify attributes with POP Wrangle or POP VOP nodes. Knowing these building blocks helps you move from simple sparks to believable sand, dust, or viscous material. By the end you should be comfortable setting up a DOP Network containing a POP Network, tuning birth rate and grain radius, and diagnosing common issues like missing colliders or mismatched node connections. Think of this as learning both the toolkit and the practical patterns that make particle simulations reliable.

keyIdea.text: Particles are many lightweight points that gain behavior through a POP Network and nodes like POP Source, POP Solver, and POP Grains to produce granular, fluid, and visual effects.

narration.text: Over the next exercises you will learn how Houdini handles particle systems through POPs and how POP Grains differs from a basic particle setup. First, you will understand what a POP Network is and how it lives inside a DOP Network, so you can organize particle logic correctly. Second, you will create and configure a POP Source to emit particles from a sphere and set birth rate, life expectancy, and initial velocity to shape your emission. Third, you will control particle motion using POP Solver and POP Force nodes such as wind, drag, and attract, and you will add colliders to make particles bounce or accumulate. Fourth, you'll implement POP Grains to make particles act like granular materials and learn to adjust radius and repulsion for piling behavior. Each objective maps to a hands-on step and a competency check so you not only know the nodes but can diagnose issues like missing node connections or inappropriate birth rates. Expect to practice attribute changes with POP Wrangle so you can vary size and color over a particle’s life and verify your simulation visually.

You will construct SOP geometry for a container and an emitter: a tube as the receiver and a small sphere elevated above it as the particle source. Next you'll wire a DOP Network that takes both SOPs as inputs and holds a POP Network. screens.title: What are POPs?
screens.subtitle: Definition and role of Particle Operators in Houdini

narration.text: POPs, short for Particle Operators, are Houdini's system for simulating many independent points that move and interact over time. Think of each particle as a lightweight point that carries attributes such as position and velocity; the POP context focuses on rules and nodes that change those attributes. POPs are not rigid bodies: particles usually behave like massless or very low-mass entities and are used where a large number of simple actors produce complex emergent motion, like smoke, sparks, or sand. A POP Network groups the nodes that control the particles; it typically lives inside a DOP Network where the simulation is advanced by a solver. A common misconception is to treat a POP Network as isolated — in practice it needs proper inputs from SOP geometry and colliders merged into the DOP so particles interact with scene objects. For example, emitting a burst of particles from a sphere and applying a POP Wind makes them stream; adding a Static Object representing a bowl causes the same particles to land and accumulate. Understanding POPs means thinking in terms of attributes and rules rather than individual objects: you design the forces and behaviors and let many particles produce the final look. How might varying the birth rate or the solver substeps change the visual result in your scene?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: POPs are node-based operators that alter particle attributes over time to create motion, interaction, and emergent effects.

content.html:
Core Concept
What are POPs?
Particle Operators for simulating many points with attributes and rules.
Quick definition
POP nodes change particle attributes like position and velocity to create motion across frames.
Why it matters
POPs let you simulate large numbers of actors efficiently, producing complex visuals from simple rules.
Common misconception
Particles are not small rigid bodies; they behave like points with attributes. Expect different collision and mass behavior than RBDs.
Illustrative cards
Emitter
POP Source provides birth, position, and initial velocity of particles.
Solver
POP Solver advances particles and applies force results each frame.
Forces
POP Wind, POP Drag and POP Attract change particle motion over time.
Grains
POP Grains add volume and repulsion, enabling piles and cohesive flows.
Key Takeaway

POPs orchestrate many points through emitters, solvers and forces; think attributes and rules rather than individual particles.

screens.title: POP Network in a DOP Network
screens.subtitle: How POPs, DOPs, SOPs and the solver connect in Houdini

narration.text: Understanding where the POP Network sits is crucial for building reliable simulations. In Houdini, POP Networks are typically created inside a DOP Network. The DOP Network is the simulation container that advances time and contains solvers and scene objects. Inside the DOP Network, the POP Network holds POP-specific nodes like POP Source and POP Grains which produce and alter particle attributes. SOP geometry is fed into the DOP Network as Static Object or RBD Packed Object nodes so particles can collide with scene geometry. A common workflow is: create SOP geometry for the emitter and colliders, route those SOP nodes into inputs on the DOP Network, place a POP Network inside the DOP, and add a POP Solver that advances particles frame-by-frame. Gravity or other force nodes are also added to the DOP and merged so the solver sees them. A common mistake is forgetting to merge the collider or not setting the correct SOP Path on the Static Object, which makes particles pass through geometry. In practice, you will test with a low birth rate and step the timeline to confirm particles emit and respond before increasing density. Which SOP paths and merge connections will you check first when particles seem to ignore colliders?

keyIdea.title: Network relationship
keyIdea.text: POP Network is placed inside a DOP Network; SOP geometry is connected as scene objects so the POP Solver can use colliders and forces.

screens.title: POP Source — Emission control
screens.subtitle: Birth Rate, Emission Type, Life Expectancy, and initial velocity

narration.text: The POP Source defines where and how particles are born, so it directly shapes the look and performance of your simulation. Emission Type chooses the geometry used for birth: scatter on surface, points, or volume. Birth Rate sets how many particles are produced per second — higher rates make denser effects but increase compute cost. Life Expectancy controls how long particles exist, which affects accumulation and memory usage. Initial velocity parameters determine the particle's starting motion; you can emit with a normal-based velocity, an explicit vector, or from another attribute. A practical example: set a sphere as your emitter, choose Surface emission, and set a Birth Rate of 5000 for a steady sand pour. If particles appear sparse, raise birth rate; if the simulation slows or memory spikes, reduce it. A typical beginner mistake is using a very high birth rate before adding colliders or grains, which makes debugging harder. Another subtle point is emission from closed geometry: ensure normals and surface orientation are correct; reversed normals can send particles inward or cause odd initial velocities. Use a small test birth rate and verify motion before moving to production rates.

keyIdea.title: Emitter control
keyIdea.text: POP Source parameters determine particle origin, quantity, lifetime, and starting motion — tune these first to shape the simulation.

content.html:
Definition
POP Source — Emission control
Set emission type, birth rate, life, and initial velocity to shape particle births.
Key parameters
  • Emission Type: surface, points, or volume
  • Birth Rate: particles per second
  • Life Expectancy: particle lifetime
  • Velocity: initial speed and direction
Checker
Start with a low birth rate, verify normals and SOP path, then increase rate for final render.
Concrete example
Emitter: Sphere
Set POP Source → Emission Type: Surface, SOP Path: /obj/pop_grains_sim/OUT_EMITTER, Birth Rate: 5000.
Tip: Use 'Scatter' for even distribution
Pitfall: Very high Birth Rate during debugging
Key Takeaway

Tune emission first: birth rate and life determine visual density; velocity shapes initial motion.

screens.title: Forces and the POP Solver
screens.subtitle: Applying wind, drag, gravity and solver behavior

narration.text: Particles move because forces change their velocity over time and the solver integrates those changes. The POP Solver advances the simulation frame by frame; it evaluates force nodes like POP Wind, POP Drag, and POP Attract each timestep. POP Wind applies directional acceleration, POP Drag reduces velocity to simulate air resistance, and POP Attract pulls particles toward a point or object. Gravity is usually added as a separate Gravity Force in the DOP Network and merged with the POP Network so the solver sees it. Solver settings and substeps matter: increasing substeps makes collisions and fast motion more stable but costs time. For example, if you emit many fast particles into a container, increasing the solver's substeps reduces tunneling through thin colliders. Use POP Drag to simulate viscous air — small drag values slow particles gradually. A common misconception is to over-rely on a single force: realistic motion comes from a combination of gravity, drag and sometimes attractors. Always test a few frames with low birth rate and check that forces behave as expected before scaling up. Forces and the POP Solver means pop solver advances particles; force nodes and gravity change velocities. tune solver substeps for stability with high-speed or dense simulations.. In practical terms, applying wind, drag, gravity and solver behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Solver and forces
keyIdea.text: POP Solver advances particles; force nodes and gravity change velocities. Tune solver substeps for stability with high-speed or dense simulations.

content.html:
Process Flow
Forces and the POP Solver
How forces change particle velocity and how the solver integrates them.
Core forces
  • POP Wind — directional push
  • POP Drag — simulates air resistance
  • POP Attract — pulls toward a point or object
  • Gravity Force — global downward acceleration (added in DOP)
Solver tuning
Adjust solver substeps to prevent tunneling and improve collision accuracy at the cost of performance.
Example and checks
Example
Emit particles downward with gravity, add small drag to slow them, and use POP Wind to bias flow when pouring into a tilted container.
Tip: Increase substeps for high-speed impacts
Pitfall: Too much drag makes motion look unnatural
Key Takeaway

Combine gravity, wind and drag thoughtfully and tune solver substeps to balance fidelity and performance.

screens.title: Collisions: Static vs Dynamic colliders
screens.subtitle: How to make particles bounce, slide, and accumulate

narration.text: Collisions determine how particles interact with scene geometry. For immovable geometry, use a Static Object node in the DOP Network and point its SOP Path to your container geometry. For moving geometry, use an RBD Packed Object so the collider itself can be simulated and respond dynamically. Inside a POP Network you can use POP Collision Detect if you need per-particle collision controls such as bounce and friction adjustments. A frequent source of error is reversed normals on the collider: inward normals on a closed container will affect collision responses and may allow particles to escape or embed. Also ensure colliders are merged into the DOP network so the POP Solver can see them. If particles pass through geometry, check that the collider node path is correct and that the solver is configured with enough substeps. For accumulation behavior, POP Grains can help particles behave as if they have volume, enabling more natural piling; without grains, particles may interpenetrate and look gaseous. A good test is to emit a modest number of particles, enable collision detection, and adjust bounce and friction to match the material you intend to simulate.

keyIdea.title: Collision types
keyIdea.text: Use Static Object for fixed colliders and RBD Packed Object for dynamic colliders. Check normals and merge inputs to ensure collisions register.

content.html:
Comparison
Collisions: Static vs Dynamic
Make particles interact with fixed or moving geometry and tune collision responses.
Static Object
Use for immovable colliders such as a container. Set SOP Path to the container geometry and ensure normals point inward if required.
RBD Packed Object
Use when the collider itself should move or break during simulation and be part of the DOP solve.
POP Collision Detect
Use in the POP Network to control bounce and friction per particle.
Checks and example
Example check
If particles pass through a tube, verify the Static Object SOP Path, reversed normals, and solver substeps.
Tip: Reverse normals for an inward-facing container
Pitfall: Missing merge of collider into DOP Network
Key Takeaway

Pick the right collider type for the job and confirm SOP paths, normals and solver settings when collisions fail.

screens.title: POP Grains: granular behavior
screens.subtitle: How POP Grains adds volume, repulsion, and piling

narration.text: POP Grains is a specialized node that gives particles granular characteristics by enforcing spacing and repulsion between neighbors. Rather than acting like point-like gas, particles with Grains gain an effective radius and try to maintain a distance from nearby particles. This produces cohesive piling and flowing behavior you would expect from sand, sugar, or small beads. Key parameters include Radius, which controls the effective particle size and therefore how they pack; and stiffness or repulsion strength, which affects how rigid the pile looks. In practice, lowering radius makes particles more likely to interpenetrate, while increasing it produces bulkier, more volume-aware motion. A hands-on use case is pouring particles from a sphere into a tube with POP Grains enabled and a Radius of 0.05 — particles will accumulate instead of passing through each other. Remember that POP Grains increases computation because neighborhood searches are required; start with lower birth rates when tuning. A misconception is thinking Grains is just a visual tweak — it fundamentally alters particle interactions, so tune it early in your setup. POP Grains: granular behavior means pop grains adds particle volume and neighbor repulsion so particles pile and flow like granular material; tune radius and strength for desired packing.. In practical terms, how pop grains adds volume, repulsion, and piling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Grains behavior
keyIdea.text: POP Grains adds particle volume and neighbor repulsion so particles pile and flow like granular material; tune radius and strength for desired packing.

content.html:
Core Concept
POP Grains: granular behavior
Introduce volume and repulsion for realistic piling and cohesive flow.
Important parameters
  • Radius — effective particle size and packing
  • Repulsion/Stiffness — strength of neighbor separation
  • Search radius — how far neighbors are considered
Performance note
Grains requires neighborhood searches; reduce birth rate while tuning to keep iteration interactive.
Example scenario
Sand pour
POP Source emits from a sphere, POP Grains with Radius 0.05 creates a pile that fills the tube rather than particles passing through each other.
Tip: Tweak radius to change packing
Pitfall: High radius with high birth rate is costly
Key Takeaway

Use POP Grains when you need particles to behave as a packed material; adjust radius and repulsion early while testing with low particle counts.

screens.title: Particle attributes and POP Wrangle
screens.subtitle: P, v, id, age — how attributes control behavior and look

narration.text: Every particle carries attributes that describe its state and can be used to drive motion and appearance. The core attributes are P for position, v for velocity, id for a unique particle identifier, and age for how long the particle has lived. You can also modify rendering-focused attributes like pscale for size and Cd for color. To programmatically adjust attributes during simulation, use a POP Wrangle or POP VOP inside the POP Network. A typical use is driving size and color over a particle's lifetime using the age attribute: age normalized from zero to lifetime can be mapped to pscale and Cd so particles shrink and fade. For example, in a POP Wrangle you might compute normalizedAge and then set @pscale = fit(normalizedAge, 0, 1, 0.1, 0.0); to make particles shrink. Remember to use the particle's id when you need stable per-particle randomization so changes persist across frames. A common misconception is to treat attributes as read-only; in POPs you often explicitly write attributes each step. Practicing attribute edits helps you transition from simulation to final shading and rendering. Particle attributes and POP Wrangle means use p, v, id, age, pscale, and cd to control motion and appearance. use pop wrangle to compute per-particle behavior.. In practical terms, p, v, id, age — how attributes control behavior and look. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Attributes matter
keyIdea.text: Use P, v, id, age, pscale, and Cd to control motion and appearance. Use POP Wrangle to compute per-particle behavior.

content.html:
Definition
Particle attributes and POP Wrangle
Attributes let you read and write particle state to control both behavior and shading.
Common attributes
  • P — position vector
  • v — velocity vector
  • id — unique identifier
  • age — lifetime progress
  • pscale, Cd — visual attributes
Best practice
Use id for stable randomness and age to drive transitions such as size or color over lifetime.
POP Wrangle example
// inside a POP Wrangle
float life = @life; // particle lifetime
float a = @age / life; // normalized age from 0 to 1
@pscale = fit(a, 0, 1, 0.1, 0.0);
@Cd = lerp({1,0.9,0.7}, {0.2,0.2,0.25}, a);
// use @id for per-particle seeded randomness
Tip: Map age to both pscale and Cd for smooth fade-out effects
Key Takeaway

Attributes are the levers for behavior and look. Use POP Wrangle to compute them every step and test with low particle counts.

screens.title: Guided lab: assemble the simulation
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step build: Tube container, Sphere emitter, DOP Network with POP Network

narration.text: Now we'll walk through the lab steps to assemble a working POP Grains simulation. First create a Geometry node named pop_grains_sim. Inside it create a Tube and set Height to 2, Radius to 1, and turn End Caps on; add a Reverse SOP to flip normals inward so particles collide correctly. Next create a Sphere, set its Radius to 0.2 and Primitive Type to Polygon, translate it up to about 2.5, and add a Null named OUT_EMITTER. Back at the object level, create a DOP Network and connect the Tube to the first input and OUT_EMITTER to the second input. Dive into the DOP Network and add a POP Network; inside the POP Network create a POP Source set to Surface and set SOP Path to /obj/pop_grains_sim/OUT_EMITTER with Birth Rate 5000. Add a POP Grains node after the source and set Radius to 0.05; then add a POP Solver and connect to the Output. Back at the DOP level, create a Static Object pointing to the reversed tube SOP path, add a Gravity Force, merge POP Network, Static Object and Gravity Force and connect to the DOP Output. Finally add a DOP Import in SOPs to fetch geometry from the popsolver for viewport playback. Test with a lower birth rate and raise it once behavior is correct.

keyIdea.title: Lab assembly
keyIdea.text: Follow SOP geometry setup, create DOP Network with POP Network, add POP Source and POP Grains, include Static Object and Gravity, then import results for playback.

Practice checkpoints

Checkpoint 2: Particles collide and accumulate inside tube

Key Takeaway

screens.title: Tuning, performance and common mistakes
screens.subtitle: Birth rate, grain radius, substeps and debugging tips

narration.text: Simulating particles is a balance between visual fidelity and performance. Birth Rate controls particle count and is often the first parameter to adjust: start low while you tune behaviors, then slowly increase for final renders. POP Grains Radius affects packing and collision; larger radius produces bulkier piles but increases neighbor search costs. Solver substeps improve accuracy for collisions and high-speed motion; increase them if particles tunnel through geometry, but expect slower simulation. Common mistakes include forgetting to merge colliders into the DOP Network, incorrect SOP paths on Static Objects, and reversed normals on container geometry. Another trap is enabling high birth rates before adding grains or collision checks, which makes results noisy and hard to debug. Use DOP Import with Fetch Geometry to view the live particle mesh and verify accumulation. Profiling tip: if simulation is slow, reduce birth rate, lower neighbor search distances in POP Grains, and only increase solver substeps when needed. Keep a small test set of particles for parameter sweeps and expand only after the behavior is correct. Tuning, performance and common mistakes means start with low birth rate, tune grain radius and solver substeps for stability, and validate sop paths and normals to avoid common mistakes.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Tuning, performance and common mistakes
Which knobs affect quality and speed, and where to look when things fail.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential ideas you should remember. First, POPs are Houdini's particle operators: they let you simulate many points that carry attributes and respond to forces. Second, the POP Network sits inside a DOP Network; SOP geometry must be connected as scene objects for collisions to register. Third, POP Source controls emission — birth rate, life expectancy and initial velocity shape the particle stream. Fourth, POP Solver and POP Force nodes advance motion and add wind, drag or attractors, while solver substeps improve stability. Fifth, POP Grains gives particles volume and repulsion so they pile and flow more realistically. Finally, particle attributes like P, v, id, and age are the levers you use to drive appearance and behavior via POP Wrangle or POP VOP. Recall the lab: create a sphere emitter and tube container, set POP Grains Radius and Birth Rate, add a Static Object and Gravity, and import results via DOP Import. Use low birth rates to tune and increase only after behavior is correct.

narration.text: A short quick-reference to keep while you experiment: First, always verify SOP paths and normals — many collision problems come from incorrect paths or inverted geometry. Second, tune emission and grains at low particle counts; birth rate and grain radius have the biggest influence on both look and performance. Third, use attributes like age and id with POP Wrangle to create per-particle variation for size and color; these small touches turn a mechanical simulation into a polished visual. Keep these checks in your workflow: verify geometry, tune gradually, and use attributes to refine appearance. These three habits will save debugging time and lead to more reliable, believable particle effects.
